claims.text: Data-driven computational optimization can be used to guide HEA processing or design.
Machine-learning-guided laser additive manufacturing can reliably fabricate three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
Dynamic adjustment of processing parameters can control NM-HEA composition.
Dynamic adjustment of processing parameters can mitigate phase segregation in NM-HEAs.
The proposed feedstock consists of near-equiatomic mixtures of noble-metal powders such as Au, Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh.
The proposed fabrication intervention is laser powder bed fusion with real-time machine-learning parameter optimization.
The process is to be conducted under an inert atmosphere with controlled substrate temperature, scan speed, and laser power.
In situ monitoring or sensor feedback can be used to adaptively tune LPBF parameters in real time.
Iterative machine-learning models can precisely control melt-pool formation, cooling rates, and elemental diffusion.
On-the-fly refinement of process variables can reduce elemental segregation.
On-the-fly refinement of process variables can promote uniform solid-solution growth.
Reduced segregation and uniform solid-solution growth can enable robust, interconnected three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
The resulting nanoframework will contain uniformly distributed multi-noble-metal catalytic sites.
The resulting nanoframework will have high surface area and improved catalytic performance.
Conventional thin-film or nanoparticle methods often cannot create scalable, interconnected three-dimensional structures with uniform composition.
Success of the approach may depend on feedstock purity and in situ sensing accuracy.
Consistency across different noble-metal combinations and scalability to larger parts remain unverified.
Experimental validation is needed to determine whether real-time adjustment consistently maintains compositional uniformity and suppresses segregation.
